traveler: John von Neumann (Neumann Janos Lajos, margittai)
title: The Apartment Above the Bank: Budapest, the Implosion Lens, and the Machine That Kept His Name
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Budapest, the House Above the Bank

stops.name: Budapest, birth on the Vaci korut
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is corrected from the research pool, whose generic Budapest centroid fell on the Buda bank rather than in Lipotvaros, and now points at the Bajcsy-Zsilinszky ut 62 corner where the birthplace plaque stands
stops.campa: In an eighteen-room apartment above the Kann-Heller offices, at the Pest corner where Vaci korut meets Bathory utca, Margit Kann bears a first son to Miksa Neumann, a banker. They name him Janos and call him Jancsi. The whole Kann clan lives in the building, grandparents and uncles and cousins on separate floors, a Jewish commercial dynasty at the height of Habsburg Budapest's confidence. Two brothers will follow him. Outside, the city is thirty years into the boom that gave it its boulevards and its bridges. The underground railway running beneath it is the first electric one on the continent.
suggested_refs: The birthplace plaque at Bajcsy-Zsilinszky ut 62, formerly Vaci korut 62, Budapest District V
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'John von Neumann'

stops.name: Budapest, the eight-digit divisions
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the year is a convention of the biographies and not a record, and the anecdotes themselves come through admirers rather than documents
stops.campa: The family stories begin early and never stop. At six he is said to divide two eight-digit numbers in his head and to trade jokes with his father in Ancient Greek. At eight he is said to have read the general history on the apartment shelves and to be able to give it back page by page. Governesses teach him German and French, and he acquires the accent in each that he will keep. None of this rests on a document. The men who worked beside him forty years later repeated some version of it for the rest of their lives.
suggested_refs: The Kann family library in the Vaci korut apartment, the setting of the recall anecdotes
sources: Popular biographical tradition repeated across encyclopedic sources

stops.name: Budapest, the emperor's patent of nobility
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Franz Joseph, in the sixty-fifth year of his reign, elevates Miksa Neumann to the Hungarian nobility for services to the economy. The family takes the predicate margittai, of Margitta, and arms with three marguerites on them. No estate comes with it and no land; the title is a purchase and a formality of the assimilated Jewish haute bourgeoisie, and the Neumanns use it lightly. The son will convert the Hungarian particle into a German one when he starts publishing from Berlin, and the world will know him by it. The emperor has three years to live and the monarchy five.
suggested_refs: The 1913 Hungarian patent of nobility granting the predicate margittai to Miksa Neumann

stops.name: Budapest, the Fasori gymnasium and the tutor at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1914 per Wikipedia, which corrects the research pool's 1911; the coordinate is corrected to the figure given in the Fasori Gimnazium article, the pool's pin having been some seven hundred metres too far north
stops.campa: He enters the Lutheran gymnasium in the Fasor. Laszlo Ratz, the mathematics master, sees within weeks what he has and goes to the father for permission to have the boy taught outside the school at university level. Gabor Szego comes to the apartment to teach the fifteen-year-old advanced calculus, because the gymnasium by its own admission can do nothing further with him. Eugene Wigner is a year ahead of him in those corridors. Edward Teller belongs to the same circle of Budapest boys.
suggested_refs: The Fasori Evangelikus Gimnazium building, Budapest District VII, and Laszlo Ratz's mathematics room

stops.name: Vienna, the flight from Bela Kun
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month of departure and the length of the absence are not documented in any reachable source
stops.campa: Bela Kun proclaims a Soviet republic in Hungary in March, and the Neumanns, bankers holding a title bought from a dead emperor, leave for Austria with the rest of their class. How long they stay is not recorded. The regime lasts a hundred and thirty-three days and is followed by Horthy's white terror and then by the numerus clausus, the first anti-Jewish university law in postwar Europe. Von Neumann is fifteen. He will speak of communism for the rest of his life in terms his American colleagues find excessive, and his biographers trace the temperature of it to this year.
suggested_refs: The 1919 Hungarian Soviet Republic and the emigre quarters of Vienna that received its refugees

segments.name: The Double Enrollment: Berlin, Zurich, Gottingen

stops.name: Berlin, two universities at once
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of both enrollments; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Miksa Neumann puts the case plainly: mathematics does not feed a man. The compromise they reach holds for five years. He matriculates in mathematics at the Pazmany Peter University in Budapest and does not attend, appearing only for examinations. He enrolls in chemistry at the University of Berlin and does attend, in the city where Einstein holds a chair and where he sits in on Erhard Schmidt's seminar. He is seventeen. His first paper, written with Michael Fekete on the zeros of certain minimal polynomials, goes to press the following year.
suggested_refs: The Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitat chemistry laboratories, Berlin, 1921-1923

stops.name: Zurich, the entrance examination at the ETH
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1923
stops.campa: He passes the entrance examination for the Eidgenossische Technische Hochschule and moves his chemistry to Zurich, where Hermann Weyl holds the mathematics chair and George Polya teaches. The chemical engineering proceeds on schedule, a filial duty discharged in laboratories with a Bunsen burner in front of him, while the work he is actually doing goes out by post to journals in Germany and Hungary. He is nineteen, and in his spare hours he is assembling an axiom system for the theory of sets.
suggested_refs: The ETH Zurich Hauptgebaude and its chemistry laboratories, 1923-1926

stops.name: Budapest, the doctorate and the definition of number
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month of the examination is not documented
stops.campa: He takes the ETH diploma in chemical engineering and in the same year presents himself at the Pazmany Peter University for doctoral examinations in mathematics, with minors in experimental physics and chemistry. The dissertation is on the axiomatic construction of set theory. He passes summa cum laude. Three years earlier he had already published the definition of ordinal number that the discipline still uses, in which each ordinal is the set of all the ordinals below it, so that number is built out of nothing except the order beneath it. He is twenty-two years old.
suggested_refs: The old main building of the Pazmany Peter University on Egyetem ter, Budapest

stops.name: Gottingen, the winter with Hilbert
stops.date_confidence: attested for the academic year 1926-1927; the coordinate is the canonical Gottingen pin already carried by the Oppenheimer and Dirac journeys and is kept byte-identical, though the mathematics institute on Bunsenstrasse lies about a kilometre northeast of it
stops.campa: A Rockefeller fellowship carries him to Gottingen for the winter, to David Hilbert, who is the reason anyone comes. Max Born's institute is across the way, and the new quantum mechanics is a few months old and quarreling with itself: Heisenberg's matrices against Schrodinger's waves, with nobody able to say why both should work. Von Neumann takes the question as a problem in the theory of operators on Hilbert space. Robert Oppenheimer arrives the same season to write a thesis under Born, Dirac and Fermi pass through, and Hilbert, whose program had demanded exactly such a formalism, is in his sixty-fifth year.
suggested_refs: The Mathematisches Institut on Bunsenstrasse and Max Born's Institut fur Theoretische Physik, Gottingen, 1926

stops.name: Berlin, the youngest Privatdozent
stops.date_confidence: attested for the habilitation date; the superlative about his age is Wikipedia's and is attributed rather than confirmed
stops.campa: He habilitates at the University of Berlin at twenty-three and begins lecturing as Privatdozent, the youngest, so the faculty's own account runs, in its history. Between 1926 and 1929 he publishes on set theory, on Hilbert's proof theory, on the ergodic problem, on almost periodic functions, and on the mathematical apparatus of quantum mechanics. At the same time he is reading economics, because a question about parlour games has caught him and will not let go of him.
suggested_refs: The habilitation records of the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitat, December 1927

stops.name: Berlin, the minimax theorem
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele appears in the Mathematische Annalen. In it he proves that every finite two-person zero-sum game has a value: each player has a way of randomizing among his options such that neither can do better by changing, and the two guarantees meet exactly in the middle. Emile Borel had posed the question a few years before and had doubted that the answer was yes. The theorem is the founding result of game theory, and sixteen years will pass before von Neumann builds the economics on top of it.
suggested_refs: 'Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele', Mathematische Annalen 100 (1928), 295-320

stops.name: Hamburg, the last German post
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the coordinate is corrected from the research pool, whose pin lay about 1.1 km west of the university near St. Pauli
stops.campa: He moves to a Privatdozent post at Hamburg, calculating openly that the German universities hold too many brilliant young men and too few chairs, and that he may wait a decade for one. Oswald Veblen writes from Princeton in the same season, offering a term of lectures on quantum theory to an American mathematics that has decided to buy itself a European faculty. Von Neumann accepts. He is twenty-five, and he expects to divide his years between two continents indefinitely. Hamburg is the last German post he holds.
suggested_refs: The Hauptgebaude of Universitat Hamburg, Edmund-Siemers-Allee 1

segments.name: Princeton, and the Chair Held for Life

stops.name: Princeton, the old Fine Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1929; the coordinate is the canonical old Fine Hall pin inherited byte-identical from dirac.journey.json, the research pool's own figure matching neither the old building nor the modern one
stops.campa: He sails in the autumn and takes up a visiting lectureship in mathematical physics at Princeton, in the Fine Hall that a later generation will call Jones Hall. Veblen is assembling a faculty out of Europe's surplus and Europe's coming refugees, and the Hungarian is the youngest and most conspicuous of the purchases. Dirac will spend the academic year 1934 in these same rooms, and Wigner arrives from Budapest by way of Berlin to a joint appointment. For the moment von Neumann keeps his German positions and crosses the Atlantic twice a year. In 1931 Princeton makes him a full professor.
suggested_refs: The old Fine Hall, now Jones Hall, Princeton University, and its common room

stops.name: Budapest, the marriage the sources cannot agree on
stops.date_confidence: contradiction preserved, not resolved: MacTutor places the wedding in 1929 before the crossing to Princeton, Wikipedia places it in 1930 after his first American term and gives no month; the date here is a placeholder for a disputed event and the coordinate is the generic Budapest centroid, no address being documented
stops.campa: He marries Mariette Kovesi in Budapest, a girl of his own quarter and his own class, and is baptized Catholic in the same season, a formality his friends record him treating as a formality. The couple sail for New Jersey. Whether the wedding falls in 1929, before he first crosses, or in 1930, after his first American term, is a question two reputable authorities answer in opposite directions, and this journey does not settle it. The marriage ends in 1937.
suggested_refs: The disagreement between MacTutor and Wikipedia over the date and sequence of the Kovesi marriage

stops.name: Berlin, the foundations of quantum mechanics
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of Springer publication; the month is conventional and the writing is split between Berlin and Princeton
stops.campa: Springer publishes Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik, begun in Berlin and finished in Princeton, and it does for quantum mechanics what Euclid did for the plane. States are unit vectors in a Hilbert space, observables are self-adjoint operators, and Heisenberg's matrices and Schrodinger's waves turn out to be one theory written in two coordinate systems. Dirac and Bohr had argued the interpretation at Solvay in 1927 with Einstein against them; von Neumann writes down the mathematics that sits underneath the argument. Robert Beyer's English translation appears at Princeton in 1955.
stops.quote: The sciences do not try to explain, they hardly even try to interpret, they mainly make models. By a model is meant a mathematical construct which, with the addition of certain verbal interpretations, describes observed phenomena.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'Method in the Physical Sciences,' in The Unity of Knowledge, ed. Lewis Leary (1955). Frequently quoted from this essay; the original text was not fetched for this journey.
suggested_refs: Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik, Springer, 1932; Beyer's English translation, Princeton University Press, 1955
sources: Princeton University Press edition, translator's note by Robert T. Beyer

stops.name: Princeton, one of the founding six
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the coordinate is the canonical Fuld Hall pin inherited byte-identical from robert_oppenheimer.journey.json
stops.campa: A department-store fortune has bought a school with no students, no examinations, and no duties, and Abraham Flexner appoints six professors of mathematics to open it. Einstein is one, arriving out of Germany in the same months. Von Neumann is another, and at twenty-nine the youngest of them. He resigns his German posts as the Nazis take the ministries, and within two years the Gottingen he studied in has been emptied of its Jews and of its physics. He holds this chair for the rest of his life. Godel will come, and Oppenheimer will direct the place after the war.
stops.quote: A large part of mathematics which becomes useful developed with absolutely no desire to be useful, and in a situation where nobody could possibly know in what area it would become useful.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'The Role of Mathematics in the Sciences and in Society' (1954), address to Princeton alumni, in Collected Works, ed. A. H. Taub, vol. VI (Pergamon, 1963). The volume itself was not fetched for this journey.
suggested_refs: Fuld Hall, Institute for Advanced Study, and the roster of the original six mathematics professors

stops.name: New York, a daughter named Marina
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the city; the research pool placed the birth at Princeton, which the Wikipedia article on Marina von Neumann Whitman contradicts
stops.campa: A daughter is born in New York and named Marina. She will become an economist. The marriage that produced her has two years left in it. The household she enters is the loudest in Princeton. Her father writes in taxis, in waiting rooms, and at other people's parties, and appears not to attend to any of it. He is thirty-one. The pure mathematics has five years left to run before the Ballistic Research Laboratory takes him, and he will not come back to it.
suggested_refs: Marina von Neumann Whitman's own memoir of her father, The Martian's Daughter

stops.name: Princeton, the house on Westcott Road
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Wikipedia confirms only that the house stood on Westcott Road, the street number 26 being biographical tradition, and the coordinate is corrected from the research pool's pin, which lay east of campus and about a kilometre and a half off the street
stops.campa: The house on Westcott Road is white clapboard and large, and the parties in it run for twenty years, drawing the Institute, the university, and whatever physicist is passing through Princeton. Von Neumann works through the noise, at a desk in the room where the noise is. Klara Dan, who becomes the second mistress of the house in 1938, sets down in an unpublished memoir the one sustained portrait of him written by somebody who lived with him. It is not the portrait his colleagues drew.
stops.quote: the strange, contradictory and controversial person; childish and good-humored, sophisticated and savage, brilliantly clever yet with a very limited, almost primitive lack of ability to handle his emotions - an enigma of nature that will have to remain unsolved.
stops.quote_source: Klara Dan von Neumann, unpublished memoir 'Grasshopper in Very Tall Grass' (c. 1962-63), quoted in George Dyson, Turing's Cathedral (Pantheon, 2012), p. 63
suggested_refs: The white clapboard house on Westcott Road, Princeton, and Klari's unpublished memoir in the von Neumann papers

stops.name: Nevada, the divorce and the citizenship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and for the state of Nevada; Reno specifically is biographical tradition carried by Macrae and Poundstone rather than record, and the pin should be read as standing for the state
stops.campa: The first marriage ends. The divorce is taken out under Nevada's residency law, which had made the state a national divorce office for anyone with money and a train ticket. Whether the proceedings were at Reno is tradition rather than record. Marina is two years old. In the same year von Neumann is naturalized as a citizen of the United States, five years before that country asks him for the mathematics of an explosion, and he keeps to the end the accent and the manners of the Vaci korut apartment.
suggested_refs: Nevada's six-week residency divorce statute and the traffic it drew in the 1930s
sources: Norman Macrae, John von Neumann (1992), cited but not opened

stops.name: Budapest, the marriage to Klara Dan
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the coordinate is the generic Budapest centroid, no venue being documented
stops.campa: He returns to Budapest in the autumn and marries Klara Dan, from his own circle in the same city, who will end her working life writing machine code for weapons calculations. The Bocher Memorial Prize of the American Mathematical Society arrives the same year, for the memoir on almost periodic functions on groups. The couple sail for America. It is very nearly the last of his crossings in this direction; Europe has some ten months of peace left, and the mathematics he has been doing for its own sake has about eighteen.
suggested_refs: The Bocher Memorial Prize citation of 1938, for the memoir on almost periodic functions on groups

stops.name: Aberdeen Proving Ground, the mathematics of things that go off
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1940 per MacTutor, which corrects the research pool's c.1937; the month is conventional
stops.campa: He joins the Scientific Advisory Committee of the Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen Proving Ground and takes up the mathematics of things that go off: shock waves, detonation fronts, the shaped charge, the behaviour of a fluid crossing from subsonic to supersonic in a few microseconds. The equations are nonlinear and nobody can solve them on paper. Out of that frustration he begins to think seriously about machines that compute. The Navy Bureau of Ordnance adds him the following year. The pure mathematician of the Institute is now a consultant to the artillery.
suggested_refs: The Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen and its differential analyser

stops.name: England, the ordnance mission the documents do not carry
stops.date_confidence: tradition only: the trip is described by Macrae and repeated after him, and no primary documentation was reachable in the research pass; the month is a guess bracketed by his return in midsummer
stops.campa: He crosses to Britain for the Navy in the first half of the year and spends some months among British ordnance scientists, on mine warfare and on the behaviour of explosives against ships and against rock. The biographers describe the journey; no document reachable for this atlas does. The stop stands on tradition. What is not in doubt is the return. He lands in the United States in the summer, and within weeks he is on a train into the mountains of northern New Mexico.
suggested_refs: Norman Macrae's account of the 1943 Navy mission to Britain, unsupported by any reachable document
sources: Norman Macrae, John von Neumann (1992), cited in the research pool but not opened

stops.name: Los Alamos, the lens that squeezes a sphere
stops.date_confidence: attested for the implosion-lens proposal of September 1943; the coordinate is the canonical Los Alamos pin inherited byte-identical from robert_oppenheimer.journey.json
stops.campa: Oppenheimer's secret city is six thousand people behind a fence, with Fermi inside it, and Bohr under the name Nicholas Baker, and Feynman picking the safes. Von Neumann arrives as a consultant and supplies the thing they cannot get. The plutonium gun will not work, and the alternative, crushing a subcritical sphere with explosives, keeps failing because the shock front arrives crooked. He proposes shaping the charge from two explosives of different detonation velocities, a lens that turns a diverging wave into a converging one. The implosion bomb becomes possible in that conversation.
stops.quote: You don't have to be responsible for the world that you're in.
stops.quote_source: Advice reportedly given to Richard Feynman at Los Alamos, recounted in Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! The source page returned 404 in the research pass and the wording is unverified.
suggested_refs: The explosive lens assemblies of the Fat Man device and the X Division implosion program

stops.name: Washington, the Target Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meetings of 27 April and 2 May 1945 and for von Neumann's membership, which corrects the research pool's blanket reconstruction tag; the coordinate is the canonical Washington pin from robert_oppenheimer.journey.json
stops.campa: The Target Committee meets twice in Washington, in the last week of April and the first days of May, military officers and Manhattan Engineer District scientists together, to choose the cities. Von Neumann is a member; that much is on the roster. The criteria go into the minutes: a large urban area, a target that blast can damage effectively, a place not yet burned by the conventional raids. That Kyoto stood on the list and that Henry Stimson personally struck it off is on the record. That von Neumann argued for Kyoto is repeated everywhere and documented nowhere this atlas could reach.
suggested_refs: The minutes of the Target Committee meetings of 27 April, 2 May and 10 May 1945

stops.name: Los Alamos, the height of burst
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meeting of 10 May 1945
stops.campa: The committee reconvenes at Los Alamos itself on the tenth of May, in the laboratory where the thing being aimed is still being built. The business of the day is the height of burst: at what altitude a given yield does the most damage over the widest area. That is a question about blast physics, and therefore a question for von Neumann. He is being asked to compute the optimum destruction of a city by a weapon whose feasibility he had supplied twenty months earlier in a room a short walk from this one. He is forty-one years old.
suggested_refs: The Los Alamos session of the Target Committee, 10 May 1945, and the height-of-burst calculations

stops.name: Trinity, the estimate spoken aloud on Compania Hill
stops.date_confidence: attested; his presence, tagged as tradition in the research pool, is documented by Ralph Carlisle Smith's record of the remark, and the coordinate is the canonical Trinity Site pin inherited from fermi.journey.json rather than a Compania Hill pin, the pool's own hill coordinate being some twenty-seven miles from ground zero in the wrong direction
stops.campa: Compania Hill holds the observers who are not needed at the shelters, twenty miles from the tower in the Jornada del Muerto. At 5:29:45 the desert goes white. Oppenheimer, at base camp, is remembering a verse in Sanskrit. Fermi is dropping torn strips of paper to read the blast wave off how far they carry. On the hill von Neumann says out loud what he takes the yield to be, in the voice he would use at a seminar, and Ralph Carlisle Smith writes it down. The lens he designed in a conference room twenty-two months earlier has worked exactly as computed.
stops.quote: that was at least 5,000 tons and probably a lot more
stops.quote_source: Von Neumann on Compania Hill, recorded by Ralph Carlisle Smith; via Wikipedia, 'Trinity (nuclear test)'
suggested_refs: Compania Hill, the VIP observation point twenty miles from the Trinity tower

segments.name: The Machine, and the Theory of Games

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Moore School and the eighteen thousand tubes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summer of 1944; the railway-platform meeting with Goldstine is a story told by the participants and is not documented
stops.campa: The story the participants tell is that Herman Goldstine, waiting for a train at Aberdeen, recognized the famous mathematician on the platform and mentioned the electronic machine going up at the Moore School. Von Neumann appears in Philadelphia soon after. ENIAC is eighteen thousand tubes and is programmed by replugging cables, a job of days. Eckert and Mauchly are already designing its successor, in which the instructions would live in the same memory as the numbers. He joins the discussions in the summer and does not leave them again in his lifetime.
stops.quote: One of his remarkable abilities was his power of absolute recall. As far as I could tell, von Neumann was able on once reading a book or article to quote it back verbatim; moreover, he could do it years later without hesitation. He could also translate it at no diminution in speed from its original language into English.
stops.quote_source: Herman H. Goldstine, The Computer from Pascal to von Neumann (Princeton University Press), p. 167
suggested_refs: The ENIAC installation at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania
sources: Herman H. Goldstine, The Computer from Pascal to von Neumann, p. 167

stops.name: Princeton, the Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Princeton University Press publishes six hundred and forty pages by von Neumann and the Viennese economist Oskar Morgenstern, who had come to the Institute in 1938 and found in residence the man whose 1928 theorem he had been citing. The book axiomatizes rational choice: utility built up out of preferences over gambles, coalitions, the value of a game to each player who plays it. Economics receives it slowly and then entirely. Morgenstern is also the man who records, five years later, Einstein telling him he comes to the Institute chiefly for the privilege of walking home with Godel.
suggested_refs: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, Princeton University Press, 1944, first edition

stops.name: Philadelphia, the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the 30 June date is the conventional one given for the circulated draft
stops.campa: Goldstine mimeographs and circulates a hundred and one pages titled First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. It describes a machine in five parts, arithmetic unit, control, memory, input, output, with the program and the data held in the same store, and it describes them in the language of idealized neurons rather than of vacuum tubes, so that the design floats free of the hardware. The draft is unfinished, it cites nobody, and it carries one name on the cover. Eckert and Mauchly's patent claims die of it. The architecture is called von Neumann's from that summer to this one.
suggested_refs: First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, mimeographed by the Moore School, June 1945

stops.name: Princeton, the design given away
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the reports; the month is conventional. The coordinate is the canonical Fuld Hall pin
stops.campa: With Arthur Burks and Goldstine he publishes the design for a parallel electronic machine of some twenty thousand operations a second, and the Institute, founded on the principle of no laboratories and no equipment, finds itself building hardware in a basement over the objections of half its faculty. The reports are deliberately not patented. Von Neumann puts the architecture into the public domain so that anyone may copy it, and within five years machines built from it are running on three continents. In the same year he speaks to the first national meeting of the Association for Computing Machinery.
stops.quote: If people do not believe that mathematics is simple, it is only because they do not realize how complicated life is.
stops.quote_source: Remark at the first national meeting of the Association for Computing Machinery, 1947, reported by Franz L. Alt, 'Archaeology of Computers: Reminiscences, 1945-1947,' Communications of the ACM 15, no. 7 (July 1972), p. 694. The ACM PDF returned 403 and Alt's text was not read directly.
suggested_refs: Burks, Goldstine and von Neumann, 'Preliminary Discussion of the Logical Design of an Electronic Computing Instrument' (1946-1947)
sources: Franz L. Alt, CACM 15 no. 7 (1972), p. 694, cited but not read

stops.name: Santa Monica, the game with no communication
stops.date_confidence: inferred: MacTutor attests the RAND consultancy across the late 1940s and the 1950s without giving a start date, and 1948 is a placeholder within that bracket
stops.campa: The Air Force's think tank on the beach at Santa Monica takes him as a consultant, and the minimax theorem of 1928 goes to work on a nuclear exchange between two powers. Two players, opposed interests, no communication, and a payoff matrix nobody wants to fill in. Von Neumann is the most hawkish of the analysts on the question of striking the Soviet Union before it has a stockpile, and the remark that follows him through every history of the Cold War is printed, in the month he is dying, in a magazine his daughter can buy at a newsstand.
stops.quote: If you say why not bomb them tomorrow, I say why not today? If you say today at five o'clock, I say why not one o'clock?
stops.quote_source: Attributed remark on preventive war against the USSR, reported in LIFE magazine, 25 February 1957. The original issue was not fetched for this journey.
suggested_refs: The RAND Corporation's early game-theoretic studies of nuclear exchange, Santa Monica
sources: LIFE magazine, 25 February 1957, cited but not fetched

stops.name: Los Alamos, MANIAC and the state of sin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the early 1950s and for the successive use of ENIAC and then the Los Alamos machine; the March 1952 date marks the completion of MANIAC I and is a placeholder for a course of repeated visits
stops.campa: The Los Alamos copy of the Princeton machine is called MANIAC, and von Neumann comes back repeatedly to run on it the thermonuclear calculations that no room of human computers could finish, having already put the first of them through ENIAC in 1945. Stanislaw Ulam works beside him, and the Monte Carlo method comes out of the collaboration: solve the deterministic problem by simulating a great many random ones. He had already put into print his objection to the way such machines make their randomness.
stops.quote: Any one who considers arithmetical methods of producing random digits is, of course, in a state of sin.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'Various Techniques Used in Connection with Random Digits,' in The Monte Carlo Method, National Bureau of Standards Applied Mathematics Series 12 (1951). The primary text returned 403/404 and was not read.
suggested_refs: MANIAC I at Los Alamos and the first Monte Carlo runs for the thermonuclear program

stops.name: Princeton, the IAS machine fully operational
stops.date_confidence: attested for 10 June 1952; the research pool's range of 1945-1951 is corrected to construction from 1946 and full operation from June 1952 per the Wikipedia article on the IAS machine
stops.campa: Construction began in 1946, and the machine is fully operational on the tenth of June 1952: forty bits in parallel, a memory of a thousand and twenty-four words held on Williams cathode-ray tubes, five kilowatts, one room in a building the Institute put up reluctantly. Its first serious work is a hydrogen bomb calculation. Its second is a numerical weather forecast, the first ever computed. Klara von Neumann writes code for it. The hardware is dismantled in 1958, and the logical design outlives every component in it.
stops.quote: His mind was just so fast and so accurate that there was no keeping up with him.
stops.quote_source: Julian Bigelow, chief engineer of the IAS machine, quoted in Ed Regis, Who Got Einstein's Office? (Addison-Wesley, 1988), pp. 103-104
suggested_refs: The IAS machine in its purpose-built room at the Institute for Advanced Study, 1952
sources: Ed Regis, Who Got Einstein's Office? (1988), pp. 103-104

segments.name: Washington, the Commission, and Walter Reed

stops.name: Washington, the General Advisory Committee and the Super
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meeting and the vote of 30 October 1949; von Neumann's role is left open, since fermi.journey.json places him on the committee itself while the standard membership lists for 1949 do not, and this journey therefore places him as an advocate outside it rather than resolving the conflict
stops.campa: The General Advisory Committee of the Atomic Energy Commission meets after the Soviet test and votes against a crash program for the hydrogen bomb, Oppenheimer in the chair, Fermi and Rabi appending an annex that calls the weapon evil in any light in which it is examined. Von Neumann is on the other side of the question and does not conceal it. Teller, out of the same Budapest generation, is with him. Truman overrides the committee in January. The split opened here is the one that will be used, five years later and in this city, to take Oppenheimer's clearance away.
suggested_refs: The GAC report of 30 October 1949 and the Fermi-Rabi minority annex

stops.name: Washington, the Teapot Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested that he chaired the Air Force's Strategic Missile Evaluation Committee; the research pool folds the chairmanship into its 1955 entry without a date of its own, and February 1954 is a placeholder inside the committee's 1953-1954 working period
stops.campa: The Air Force asks him to chair the Strategic Missile Evaluation Committee, which everyone involved calls the Teapot Committee, on the question of whether an intercontinental ballistic missile is worth building. The answer turns on whether a thermonuclear warhead can be made light enough to fly, and von Neumann, who knows the weapon physics and the numerical methods both, says that it can. The committee's report starts the Atlas program. He is by now advising more agencies than he can visit in a week, and spends most of the week on aeroplanes.
suggested_refs: The report of the Strategic Missile Evaluation Committee and the origin of the Atlas program

stops.name: Washington, sworn in to the Atomic Energy Commission
stops.date_confidence: attested for 15 March 1955
stops.campa: Eisenhower nominates him to the Atomic Energy Commission and the Senate confirms. He resigns the Institute professorship he has held for twenty-two years and moves to Washington to become one of five men with authority over the American nuclear enterprise. He is fifty-one. In the same year he writes an essay for a business magazine asking whether technology can be survived at all. The answer he gives is that no arrangement made in advance can make it safe.
stops.quote: For progress there is no cure. Any attempt to find automatically safe channels for the present explosive variety of progress must lead to frustration. The only safety possible is relative, and it lies in an intelligent exercise of day-to-day judgment.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'Can We Survive Technology?', Fortune magazine, 1955. The original Fortune text was not fetched for this journey.
suggested_refs: 'Can We Survive Technology?', Fortune, June 1955

stops.name: Washington, the mass at the collarbone
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1955; the month is not documented and the primary site of the cancer is given as bone in some accounts and pancreatic in others, a contradiction this journey does not resolve
stops.campa: A mass is found near his collarbone and the biopsy comes back metastasized. Which organ it started in is answered two different ways by two sets of accounts. He has watched bomb tests at close range and worked fifteen years among materials whose hazards nobody had measured, and whether the one caused the other is a question his colleagues asked at once and nobody has answered since. He stays at the Commission. Within months he cannot walk, and the meetings come to him instead.
suggested_refs: The disputed etiology of von Neumann's cancer and its supposed link to Trinity and to Operation Crossroads
sources: Ananyo Bhattacharya, The Man from the Future (2021), cited but not opened

stops.name: Walter Reed, the wheelchair and the first Fermi Award
stops.date_confidence: attested that he worked from Walter Reed through 1956 and received both the Medal of Freedom and the inaugural Enrico Fermi Award that year; the month is a placeholder, and the research pool's White House ceremony venue is dropped as unattested
stops.campa: He is moved into a suite at Walter Reed and continues Commission business from it in a wheelchair. Eisenhower gives him the Medal of Freedom in that condition, and the Atomic Energy Commission gives him the Enrico Fermi Award, the first ever conferred. A guard is said to have been posted at his door on the reasoning that a sedated man who holds the whole American weapons program in his head might say any part of it out loud; that story rests on the biographies and on no document that has surfaced. He asks for a Catholic priest.
stops.quote: There probably is a God. Many things are easier to explain if there is than if there isn't.
stops.quote_source: Attributed deathbed-era remark, reported in Norman Macrae, John Von Neumann (1992). Secondhand, and not verified against Macrae's text.
suggested_refs: The 1956 Medal of Freedom citation and the inaugural Enrico Fermi Award

stops.name: Walter Reed, the eighth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies in the hospital room in Washington, fifty-three years old, having spent eighteen months unable to work at the speed that had been the whole instrument of his life, and having found that unbearable, by the account of those who visited him. Wigner, who had walked the same gymnasium corridors in Budapest forty-three years earlier and had gone on to a Nobel Prize, writes the memoir for the American Philosophical Society. He does not soften it. The mind he describes in it was not a comfortable one to be near.
stops.quote: A mind of von Neumann's inexorable logic had to understand and accept much that most of us do not want to accept and do not even wish to understand.
stops.quote_source: Eugene P. Wigner, 'John von Neumann (1903-1957),' Year Book of the American Philosophical Society (1958); reprinted in Symmetries and Reflections (Indiana University Press, 1967), p. 261
suggested_refs: Wigner's biographical memoir of von Neumann for the American Philosophical Society, 1958
sources: Eugene P. Wigner, Symmetries and Reflections (1967), p. 261

segments.name: The Posthumous Books and the Crater

stops.name: Princeton Cemetery, the grave with two coordinates
stops.date_confidence: attested for the cemetery; the exact day of burial is not documented and is given as four days after the death. The coordinate is Wikipedia's figure for Princeton Cemetery, in place of two conflicting figures carried by this atlas's own research lenses
stops.campa: He is buried at Princeton Cemetery, a few streets from the university where he first taught in America and a short walk from the Institute where he held his chair for twenty-two years. Two different positions for this grave circulate in the atlas's own files; the cemetery's own coordinate is used here and the disagreement is left standing. The claim that he lies in the Presidents' Plot is wrong and is dropped. The Institute closes its computer project the year after his death, on the grounds that building machines was never the business of a school with no laboratories.
suggested_refs: The von Neumann family plot at Princeton Cemetery, Witherspoon Street

stops.name: New Haven, the lectures he could not deliver
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Yale had invited him to give the Silliman Lectures and he had accepted, and then he could not travel, and then he could not write. The manuscript is published unfinished. It sets the nervous system beside computing machinery at the points where the comparison can be made in numbers: how many elements, how fast, how precise, and how deep a chain of logic a system can run before its errors swamp the answer. His conclusion is that the brain does not compute the way his machines do and that whatever language it uses is not the one mathematics has been writing in.
suggested_refs: The Computer and the Brain, Yale University Press, 1958, the unfinished Silliman Lecture manuscript

stops.name: Urbana, the machine that copies itself
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Arthur Burks finishes from lecture notes and drafts the book von Neumann left in pieces, and the University of Illinois publishes it nine years after his death. In it a machine sits on an infinite grid of cells, each cell in one of twenty-nine states, and carries a description of itself, and builds a copy that carries the description too, and so reproduces. He had asked what the logical minimum for self-reproduction is, before anyone knew the structure of DNA, and had answered that the thing must hold a tape of instructions that is both executed and copied blind.
suggested_refs: Theory of Self-Reproducing Automata, ed. Arthur W. Burks, University of Illinois Press, 1966
sources: University of Illinois Press edition, ed. Arthur W. Burks, 1966

stops.name: The Moon, the far side, a walled plain named
stops.date_confidence: attested for the IAU approval in 1970, which corrects the research pool's vague mid-century dating; the month is conventional and the coordinate is selenographic rather than terrestrial
stops.campa: On the far side of the Moon, at forty degrees north and a hundred and fifty-three degrees east, there is a walled plain seventy-five kilometres across, on ground no human being had ever seen until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959. It was catalogued as Crater 58 until the International Astronomical Union approved a name for it in 1970. The naming falls thirteen years after his death. The machines that computed the trajectories of the probes and the landings were built on the architecture he had put into the public domain rather than patent.
suggested_refs: Von Neumann crater, lunar far side, 40 17 N 153 15 E, IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature

stops.name: Kecskemet, the nation takes the name back
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the founding merger; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Hungary merges the colleges of the Great Plain into a single university and names it Neumann Janos Egyetem, claiming for the nation the boy who left it at seventeen and afterwards came back only to be married. The joke about the Martians is older than the university and did not come from colleagues baffled by Hungarian brilliance. Leo Szilard supplied it himself, in answer to Fermi asking where the extraterrestrials had got to: they are already here among us, they just call themselves Hungarians.
suggested_refs: Neumann Janos Egyetem, Kecskemet, founded 2016; Gyorgy Marx, The Voice of the Martians
sources: Hungarian government founding decree / university records
